title: Future-Proofing Your Law Firm: Lessons from AI Benchmarking — full episode transcript
pub: AI and the Future of Law / 2030 Vision, American Arbitration Association
author: Jen Leonard · Bridget McCormack

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: The source shares the cluster’s concern that lawyer development and mentoring are inadequate, but reframes AI primarily as scaffolding and an opportunity to accelerate junior capability, broaden practice and improve engagement. It does not adopt the cluster’s central competence paradox or its emphasis on preserving independent practice and deliberately reconstructing apprenticeship; instead, it suggests that access to AI and experimentation may address existing training weaknesses.
qs: Bridget McCormack: It opens up a huge opportunity to rethink how we structure firms and train lawyers.
They don’t need huge changes—just access to these tools.

st.t: Production model: Institutional absorption governs AI value
st.an: The source aligns with the cluster’s discussion of disrupted junior development and a possible shift toward generalist capability, but presents both as tentative extrapolations rather than measured legal-practice effects. It does not address the cluster’s principal claim that institutional absorption, workflow redesign, verification and accountability govern AI value.
qs: If a first- or second-year associate can now do the work of an eighth- or ninth-year, what does that mean for development?
But maybe the generalist lawyer—the one-stop-shop down the street—is coming back.

st.t: Delivery economics: AI pressures pricing and apprenticeship
st.an: The source accepts that AI may disrupt traditional associate development and materially extends the cluster by proposing AI-enabled generalist practice, cross-disciplinary teams and greater experimentation in professional development. It treats these as opportunities rather than demonstrated outcomes and does not address pricing or provide a settled apprenticeship model.
qs: Bridget McCormack: It opens up a huge opportunity to rethink how we structure firms and train lawyers.

st.t: Law-firm pyramid: Efficiency threatens revenue and training
st.an: The source accepts the prospect that AI could disrupt junior development and materially extends the cluster’s workforce-change argument by proposing accelerated associate capability and a possible shift from specialist teams toward AI-assisted generalists. These are conditional hypotheses, not evidence of realised staffing or training outcomes, and the source does not address the cluster’s revenue, leverage, pricing or buyer-side claims.
qs: If a first- or second-year associate can now do the work of an eighth- or ninth-year, what does that mean for development?
But maybe the generalist lawyer—the one-stop-shop down the street—is coming back.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core copilot framing: AI should offload bounded, low-stakes work while preserving human capacity for judgment-intensive tasks. It materially extends the synthesis by exploring how AI-enabled capability gains and expertise transfer could reshape junior development, specialization and the generalist-lawyer model, while correctly treating those consequences as unresolved predictions rather than established outcomes.
qs: But there are also so many low-stakes, time-intensive tasks that can be offloaded to AI, freeing up human capacity for the work that truly needs it.
If a first- or second-year associate can now do the work of an eighth- or ninth-year, what does that mean for development?

st.t: Practitioner engagement: Redesign should precede technological certainty
st.an: The source accepts practitioner experimentation and redesign while materially extending the cluster’s reliability agenda through independent, task-specific benchmarking against a human-lawyer baseline. It also calls for measuring lawyers’ own effectiveness and treats demonstrations, junior-development claims and revived generalism as prompts for investigation rather than established outcomes.
qs: Each tool’s output was measured for accuracy, and VALS partnered with Cognia Law—an ALSP—to source human lawyers who also completed these tasks.

st.t: Selective augmentation: Verification constrains uneven productivity gains
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core hybrid, task-specific approach and materially extends it with independent Vals AI benchmarking showing that AI can outperform imperfect human baselines on several structured tasks while humans retain advantages in judgment-intensive work. It also develops the cluster’s junior-development theme by proposing AI-supported learning and experimentation with team structures, though these organisational claims remain largely speculative.
qs: And we’re already working in hybrid mode, combining AI and human intelligence whether we admit it or not.
Humans still did better in certain tasks—like redlining and contract review—probably because those require more judgment about what to focus on.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: The source accepts the core idea that AI will reshape lawyers’ work and development rather than simply eliminate lawyers. It materially extends the cluster by proposing that AI-enabled expertise transfer could compress the junior–senior capability gap and weaken practice-area silos, potentially reviving broader generalist practice. These legal-sector implications are framed as hypotheses, not demonstrated outcomes.
qs: If a first- or second-year associate can now do the work of an eighth- or ninth-year, what does that mean for development?
One lawyer, aided by AI, might now be able to cover all those areas.

st.t: Service redesign: Resistance reflects incentives and identity
st.an: The source accepts that legal AI requires redesign of firms, training and adoption practices rather than mere tool acquisition. It materially extends the cluster by proposing AI-supported development for junior lawyers and personally relevant demonstrations as mechanisms for overcoming anxiety and resistance, while treating broader capability gains as task-dependent or speculative.
qs: Bridget McCormack: It opens up a huge opportunity to rethink how we structure firms and train lawyers.
But if they see something applied to work they personally care about, it can change everything.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core account of uneven, task-specific capability, hybrid human–AI work and the need to redesign firms and lawyer development. It materially extends that account by arguing for human-performance baselines, client-centred speed–cost–accuracy trade-offs, and possible shifts toward broader generalist practice, while treating long-term developmental effects as unresolved.
qs: The AIs were strongest with structured, text-based tasks—not open-ended research.
Bridget McCormack: It opens up a huge opportunity to rethink how we structure firms and train lawyers.

st.t: Expertise pipeline: Automated work weakens succession routes
st.an: The source accepts that AI may disrupt established lawyer-development pathways by enabling juniors to perform more senior work and weakening practice-area boundaries. It supports rethinking firm structure and professional development, while presenting generalist practice and experimentation as possibilities rather than demonstrated solutions or a concrete training model.
qs: If a first- or second-year associate can now do the work of an eighth- or ninth-year, what does that mean for development?
Bridget McCormack: It opens up a huge opportunity to rethink how we structure firms and train lawyers.

st.t: Professional engagement: Lawyers should shape AI deployment
st.an: The source directly supports engagement through practical, relevant demonstrations and reinforces the cluster’s caution that enthusiasm should not substitute for evidence. Its call to measure lawyers’ effectiveness aligns with the cluster’s learning-and-testing agenda rather than materially extending it.
qs: But if they see something applied to work they personally care about, it can change everything.

st.t: Professional tasks: Partial credit overstates complete success
st.an: The source endorses independent, task-specific evaluation of legal-AI tools and describes firm-defined professional tasks assessed for accuracy against lawyers completing the same work. This aligns with the cluster’s rejection of broad competence claims based on reputation or fluency, though the excerpt provides no results or analysis of partial-credit versus complete-task success.
qs: Researchers partnered with firms like Reed Smith, Fisher Phillips, McDermott Will & Emery, and Ogletree Deakins to define tasks for the AI tools, including: Data extraction, Document Q&A, Summarization, Redlining, Transcript analysis, Chronology generation, and EDGAR research.
Each tool’s output was measured for accuracy, and VALS partnered with Cognia Law—an ALSP—to source human lawyers who also completed these tasks.

st.t: Task substitution: Complementarity can still reshape staffing
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core possibility that AI may complement individual lawyers while substituting for work previously requiring more senior lawyers or multiple specialists, thereby reshaping development and staffing. Its claims about accelerated junior capability and generalist practice are explicitly conditional extrapolations, not demonstrated employment outcomes.
qs: If a first- or second-year associate can now do the work of an eighth- or ninth-year, what does that mean for development?
One lawyer, aided by AI, might now be able to cover all those areas.

kp.k: Personal demonstrations can overcome barriers to AI adoption
kp.d: McCormack describes showing a T14 law-school academic DeepResearch output on the interstate eviction-law question the academic had investigated with student researchers. Output arrived twenty minutes later and impressed the academic; the anecdote illustrates adoption through personally relevant demonstrations, not a verified comparison of research quality. McCormack identifies even subscribing to a tool as a barrier for hesitant users.
qs: Twenty minutes later, I showed her the output. She was stunned—literally calling over her partner, amazed at what she was seeing.
For people who feel hesitant or overwhelmed, even just signing up for a subscription is a big barrier.

kp.k: Low-stakes automation could expand public-service capacity
kp.d: Leonard recounts Claude helping a public-service friend prepare a press release, talking points, anticipated objections, accessible language and a 30-day social-media calendar. She argues that automating time-intensive, low-stakes work could free overburdened public servants for work requiring human attention, while noting government access restrictions and concerns about AI use on high-stakes issues affecting vulnerable populations.
qs: I remember when I worked in government—so many tools were blocked, firewalled, or unavailable.
But there are also so many low-stakes, time-intensive tasks that can be offloaded to AI, freeing up human capacity for the work that truly needs it.

kp.k: AI workarounds challenge conventional education and hiring assessments
kp.d: The hosts discuss secondhand stories of students concealing AI assistance in assignments and live technical hiring tests. McCormack interprets these workarounds as evidence of outdated assessments and future technological competence; Leonard draws an analogy to assessments in law. Their approval and McCormack's prediction that such students will run companies in five years are opinions, not measured educational or employment findings.
qs: He developed a tool that uses generative AI to solve the problems and subtly show him the answers without moving his eyes—so the proctor wouldn’t notice.
It’s not a meaningful way to assess talent anymore.
I couldn't help but think of similar outdated assessments in our own industry.
Those are the students who are going to run the companies in five years.

kp.k: Cross-domain experiment suggests AI can substitute for small teams
kp.d: Discussing The Cybernetic Teammate, McCormack reports a Procter & Gamble field experiment involving R&D and business-development participants working on real product challenges, alone or in two-person teams, with some paired with GPT-4. The researchers measured performance, expertise sharing and emotional experience. She reports that AI-assisted individuals matched or exceeded teams without AI and that AI improved productivity and innovation. These are reported findings from business work, not demonstrated legal-task results.
qs: The researchers worked with two teams at Procter & Gamble—one R&D team and one business development team—on real product challenges.
Some participants worked alone, others in two-person teams, and some were paired with GPT-4.
For performance, individuals paired with AI performed as well as—or better than—teams without AI.

kp.k: AI reportedly bridges expertise silos and improves work experience
kp.d: McCormack reports that AI balanced missing expertise across P&G's technical and commercial functions and that participants experienced more positive and fewer negative emotions, with greater engagement and less anxiety and frustration. Leonard connects this to her own experience and a previously discussed University of Minnesota study in which law students reportedly enjoyed AI-assisted work more; the transcript supplies no further study details for that comparison.
qs: On expertise sharing, the AI helped bridge knowledge silos. It balanced out missing expertise on teams and acted like a shortcut.
Participants using AI reported more positive emotions and fewer negative ones. They were more engaged, less anxious, and less frustrated than those working without AI.
It also echoes that University of Minnesota study we talked about—law students using AI reported enjoying the work more.

kp.k: Cross-functional AI could revive generalist legal practice
kp.d: Leonard reports that Claude and ChatGPT, prompted about the P&G study's legal implications, suggested AI might let one lawyer cover tax, real estate and M&A rather than assembling separate specialists. McCormack speculates that generalist practice could return, improving quality of life, access to justice and the sustainability of small-town or rural practices. Leonard suggests broader offerings for solo and small firms and a possible rebalancing from corporate law toward people law; these are extrapolations, not legal-market findings.
qs: Both Claude and ChatGPT pointed out that in a legal context, this could dissolve practice area boundaries.
One lawyer, aided by AI, might now be able to cover all those areas.
Better for quality of life, better for access to justice, and more sustainable for small-town or rural practices.
And maybe it pushes back on what Bill Henderson’s talked about for decades: the shift from “people law” to “corporate law.”

kp.k: Capability gains could reshape associate development and team design
kp.d: Following her AI-assisted interpretation of the P&G research, Leonard asks what development would mean if first- or second-year associates could perform eighth- or ninth-year work, and whether associates might work across disciplines alongside partners and AI. McCormack endorses rethinking firm structure and training and sees professional-development programs as less constrained than law schools. The discussion raises possibilities rather than establishing equivalent associate competence or specifying a new staffing ratio.
qs: If a first- or second-year associate can now do the work of an eighth- or ninth-year, what does that mean for development?
Will we see associates working across disciplines, with partners and AI as part of the team?
And unlike law schools, PD programs aren’t constrained in the same way. There’s so much room for experimentation.

kp.k: AI scaffolding could supplement strained legal mentoring systems
kp.d: The hosts describe confusion and embarrassment during law school and limited partner capacity to mentor juniors in high-stakes practice. Leonard proposes using AI to explain sample exams and supply background, especially for first-generation students and those unfamiliar with legal culture. She argues that access to tools could reduce anxiety and increase engagement, while identifying billable-hour pressures and partners' lack of teaching preparation as existing constraints.
qs: But now? I’d upload that sample to Claude and ask, “What’s good about this? Walk me through it.”
Just some background, some scaffolding—especially for first-gen students or anyone new to legal culture.
They’re trying to teach you on top of billable hours in a system that never taught them how to train anyone.
If we can reduce anxiety and increase engagement, we can help junior lawyers unlock their own potential.

kp.k: VALS benchmarking compares legal tools against human task performance
kp.d: Leonard describes a VALS report released the previous month as an independent evaluation of Harvey's Assistant, Thomson Reuters' CoCounsel, vLex's Vincent AI and VECFLOW's Oliver; Lexis+ AI withdrew before tasks began. Reed Smith, Fisher Phillips, McDermott Will & Emery and Ogletree Deakins helped define extraction, document Q&A, summarization, redlining, transcript analysis, chronology and EDGAR research tasks. Cognia Law, identified as an ALSP, supplied lawyers for an accuracy baseline. McCormack calls it the first real legal benchmarking study, a characterization made by the speaker.
qs: Lexis+ AI was originally included but withdrew before the tasks began.
Each tool’s output was measured for accuracy, and VALS partnered with Cognia Law—an ALSP—to source human lawyers who also completed these tasks. Their performance served as a baseline.
Without it, we’re just comparing AI tools to each other. But the human benchmark shows us what we’re really working with—and what’s possible.

kp.k: Reported benchmark results favor AI on many bounded tasks
kp.d: McCormack reports that AI tools performed slightly better than lawyers in most categories, while humans did better on redlining and contract review. Leonard gives data-extraction accuracy of 75.1% for Harvey and 73.2% for CoCounsel. McCormack attributes human advantages tentatively to judgment about what matters and predicts tools could catch up with training; the transcript provides no numerical human accuracy baseline.
qs: In most categories, the AI tools performed slightly better than the human lawyers.
Humans still did better in certain tasks—like redlining and contract review—probably because those require more judgment about what to focus on.
Harvey was 75.1% accurate at data extraction, CoCounsel was 73.2%, etc.
But even there, it feels like the tools could catch up quickly with training.

kp.k: Hallucinations and judgment limitations qualify benchmark enthusiasm
kp.d: Leonard explicitly reports continuing hallucinations, difficulty with complex legal judgment and variation by document type. She characterizes structured, text-based work as stronger than open-ended research. These qualifications limit the scope of the hosts' broader claims that tools are already matching or surpassing lawyers.
qs: Some tools struggled with complex legal judgment.
Hallucinations still happened, and performance varied based on document type.
The AIs were strongest with structured, text-based tasks—not open-ended research.

kp.k: Client outcomes motivate hybrid work and accuracy tradeoffs
kp.d: Leonard relays Jason Barnwell's criticism of assumptions about flawless human work and binary human-versus-machine choices. She argues hypothetically that a client may prefer 95% accuracy in five minutes to 100% in 20 hours and says hybrid work is already occurring. McCormack supplies an investor's anecdotal preference for prompt dispute resolution rather than perfection. These examples express possible client priorities, not measured preferences or benchmark results.
qs: A client may prefer 95% accuracy in five minutes over 100% in 20 hours.
And we’re already working in hybrid mode, combining AI and human intelligence whether we admit it or not.
“Tell me what we owe so we can move forward.”
Lawyers often see themselves as the centerpiece when sometimes, we’re just the bottleneck.

kp.k: Benchmarking supports accountability but may become less salient
kp.d: Leonard says benchmarking currently matters for transparency and accountability, including at AAA, but speculates that it might feel irrelevant in five years. McCormack agrees that comparisons build confidence during early adoption and suggests their perceived necessity could fade once AI is integrated and normalized. Neither presents evidence that benchmarking will actually cease.
qs: It matters now, especially for organizations like AAA that need to show transparency and accountability.
But in five years? It might feel irrelevant.
Once the tech is fully integrated and normalized, the need to compare might fade.

kp.k: Response-length comparisons prompt scrutiny of lawyers' effectiveness
kp.d: Leonard reports that a data-extraction chart showed AI responses averaging 2,000 to 3,000 characters against nearly 16,000 for lawyers, interpreting this as excessive human verbosity. The hosts use the comparison to argue that the profession inadequately measures its own effectiveness and should study legal work rather than presume human superiority.
qs: AI responses averaged 2,000 to 3,000 characters. Lawyers? Nearly 16,000.
We say the same thing—but in eight times as many words.
You’re the one who always says: for a profession obsessed with evidence and proof, we don’t study what we do—or whether it works. We don’t even measure our own effectiveness.
We really don’t. But we should.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: AI tools already match or exceed lawyers on some bounded tasks, with remaining weaknesses in judgment-intensive work.
pts.d: McCormack interprets the Vals AI evaluation as showing slightly better AI performance in most tested categories, while humans remain stronger at redlining and contract review. She predicts that training could close those remaining gaps quickly. Leonard describes rapid improvement but also reports hallucinations, document-dependent performance and weaknesses in complex judgment and open-ended research. These are the speakers' interpretations of the reported benchmark, not a claim that AI surpasses lawyers across all legal work.

pts.k: AI could accelerate junior lawyers' capabilities and enable individual lawyers to work across practice boundaries.
pts.d: Leonard presents potential capability leaps for junior associates as a question, rather than an established finding. Drawing on responses she solicited from Claude and ChatGPT about a cross-functional business experiment, she suggests one AI-assisted lawyer might cover tax, real estate and M&A work. McCormack speculates that this could revive generalist practice. Leonard further suggests that AI could support cross-disciplinary staffing and a rebalancing toward individual-client legal services. These are legal-sector extrapolations, not measured results from the business experiment.

pts.k: AI assistance could improve legal training, reduce anxiety and provide explanatory support where human mentoring is limited.
pts.d: Leonard argues that access to AI could increase junior lawyers' engagement and help them develop their potential. Both speakers imagine AI providing the contextual explanation they lacked in law school. They identify professional development as an opportunity for experimentation, especially given partners' limited time and training as mentors. Their legal-development claims combine personal recollections with reported research on emotional experience, rather than evidence of long-term lawyer development outcomes.

pts.k: AI-assisted research and routine public-service work can expand human capacity.
pts.d: McCormack describes a rapid DeepResearch demonstration concerning comparative state eviction law as evidence of research assistance that can change users' willingness to adopt AI. Leonard describes Claude generating public-initiative communications and argues that offloading lower-stakes tasks could let overburdened public servants serve more people with less burnout. Neither anecdote establishes independently verified legal accuracy or quantified productivity gains.

pts.k: Hybrid human–AI services and client preferences may shift attention from perfection toward speed and resolution.
pts.d: Leonard asserts that hybrid working is already occurring and offers a hypothetical client preference for faster, somewhat less accurate service. McCormack's account of an investor wanting a dispute resolved supports her suggestion that perfect resolution is not always a client's overriding priority. The numerical accuracy/time comparison is illustrative, not an observed service outcome or surveyed preference.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The main legal-performance evidence is a reported independent Vals AI benchmark with a human-lawyer baseline.
pts.d: Leonard identifies Harvey's Assistant, Thomson Reuters' CoCounsel, vLex's Vincent AI and VECFLOW's Oliver as evaluated products, and says Lexis+ AI withdrew before testing. Law firms helped define tasks encompassing extraction, document Q&A, summarization, redlining, transcript analysis, chronology generation and EDGAR research. Cognia Law, an ALSP, supplied human lawyers for the baseline. Leonard reports data-extraction accuracy of 75.1% for Harvey and 73.2% for CoCounsel, and shorter AI responses. The transcript does not provide full scores, sample sizes or methodological detail.

pts.k: Cross-domain experimental findings underpin, but do not directly test, the legal-team predictions.
pts.d: McCormack and Leonard discuss The Cybernetic Teammate, attributed to Ethan Mollick and colleagues. As described, P&G participants worked on real product challenges alone or in cross-functional teams, with or without GPT-4. Outcomes concerned performance, expertise sharing and emotional experience. McCormack reports that AI-assisted individuals matched or exceeded unaided teams and that AI improved cross-specialty knowledge sharing and emotions. Leonard's proposed implications for legal specialization and junior capability were also informed by model-generated interpretations of that study.

pts.k: Additional support consists of user demonstrations, personal experience and briefly referenced research.
pts.d: McCormack's eviction-law research demonstration and Leonard's public-service communications demonstration supply anecdotal adoption and capability evidence. Both draw on their own law-school anxiety and workplace mentoring experiences. Leonard references a University of Minnesota study on law students' enjoyment of AI-assisted work without giving its methods or numerical results. She also invokes research associated with Marty Seligman and David Epstein to support generalist work, without detailing its application to law.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Current task-level capability is distinguished from conditional future changes to professional roles.
pts.d: In this 2025 episode, Leonard describes the Vals AI report as released the previous month. McCormack characterizes task-level parity as already present roughly three years into the technology's development and suggests judgment-task improvement could occur quickly with training, without a definite deadline. Generalist revival, cross-disciplinary teams and accelerated associate capability remain possibilities conditional on AI transferring expertise into legal practice. Current performance is qualified by hallucinations, document type and task complexity.

pts.k: Adoption depends on access and demonstration; benchmarking may become less salient after normalization.
pts.d: The speakers identify subscription hesitancy and government tool restrictions as present adoption barriers. Leonard frames access as an immediate opportunity for junior-lawyer support. Separately, she speculates that benchmarking could feel irrelevant in five years, while McCormack makes declining comparison needs conditional on full integration and normalization. They still describe benchmarking as important now for confidence, transparency and accountability.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Solo, small-town and rural practices could broaden services, potentially benefiting people with unmet legal needs.
pts.d: McCormack links a possible generalist revival to quality of life, access to justice and rural-practice sustainability. Leonard identifies expanded offerings for solo and small practices and a possible rebalancing from corporate law toward 'people law.' These are prospective benefits rather than measured access-to-justice outcomes.

pts.k: Students, junior lawyers, partners and firm leaders face potential changes in learning, mentoring and team design.
pts.d: The speakers particularly emphasize first-generation students and people unfamiliar with legal culture, who could gain contextual explanations from AI. Junior associates might gain capability and confidence, while partners and professional-development teams could experiment with AI-supported training. Firm leaders could reconsider specialty boundaries and team organization. The episode does not quantify staffing reductions or specify a new leverage ratio.

pts.k: Clients, dispute-resolution organizations, researchers and public servants could experience faster work and expanded capacity.
pts.d: Leonard suggests clients may prioritize prompt resolution over marginal accuracy gains. AAA is identified as an organization for which current benchmarking supports transparency and accountability. Academic researchers are portrayed as gaining substantial research assistance, while public servants and the people they serve could benefit from faster communications and less administrative burden. These public-service benefits are distinct from the episode's separate access-to-justice predictions.
